title: Position importance in NCAA football
author: Zachary Knowlton (Oracle Data Cloud), Gilbert W. Fellingham (BYU Statistics)
source_pdf: G:/My Drive/GSE-Research/sports-research-papers/2017 Position importance in NCAA football - Zachary Knowlton and Gilbert W. Fellingham.pdf
source_note: Journal of Sports Analytics 3 (2017) 119-127, DOI 10.3233/JSA-170130, IOS Press, open access CC BY-NC 4.0, 9 pages, full read via pymupdf. Identity confirmed (Knowlton/Fellingham, zacharyknowlton21@gmail.com). Domain football (catalog correct). Model equations print with stacked fractions/Greek; reconstructed as labeled LaTeX from clean prose; 22 pure-prose quotes verified. Data: 2015 BYU season; coaches' per-play grades (defense minus/plus -> 0/1 assignment-sound; offense 0/1/2 failed/average/exceptional); expected points E(Pts) via White-Berry (2002) tiered polychotomous regression on FBS 2005-2013 (down/distance/field position); ΔE(Pts) per play (Kovash-Levitt 2009), example 0.22->1.49=1.27. Model: y_i=ΔE(Pts)~N(μ_i,σ²_y); μ_i=β0k+Σβ_jk x_ij; β_jk~N(θ_z,ξ_z) (player borrows from position); θ_z~N(0,2) common prior; ξ_z,σ²_y~Gamma(4,2) (mean 2 var 1); β0k~N(-1,2); MCMC/JAGS. Importance IS=mean/sd (Miskin 2010). Results: offense QB IS 0.19 highest (E θ 0.26, sd 1.34, variability from teammate dependence), RB/WR next; defense BoundCB 2.70 > Mike 1.96 > RE 1.61; Mike play-calling communication externality; BoundCB big-play tail risk; β0o Boise +0.56 vs Mizzou -2.06; β0d win -1.86 vs loss -2.65; win = more grouped (consistent) position effects. 13 defensive positions (2 empty/play modeled for formation); multi-position players separate β; defensive ΔE sign-flipped (positive coeff = value for BYU). Limitations: not all games graded (missing Nebraska/UCLA/Wagner/Utah State/Utah offense, Wagner/Utah defense); coach grades not well calibrated. Proprietary player data -> only position estimates published. Applications: recruiting focus, player tie-breaks, skill importance. No sportsbook lines used as model inputs.

primitives.name: Expected points E(Pts) from down, distance, field position (White-Berry)
primitives.verbatim_quote: we first used the model developed by White and Berry (2002) to find the average eventual points or expected points, denoted by E(Pts), a team should score based on the starting position of each play relative to down, distance, and field position.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.E(Pts): expected eventual points from a play state [points]

assumptions: Expected points is the average eventual points a team should score from a play's starting state
It is estimated by the White-Berry tiered polychotomous regression on FBS 2005-2013 play-by-play
primitives.breakdown_regime: E(Pts) ranges roughly -2 to +5; it is a state-value function over down/distance/field-position, the foundation the per-play delta is built on.

layer2.mapping: GSE expected-points state value IS this E(Pts) model: the engine computes a state-value function over down/distance/field-position giving expected eventual points, the expected-points foundation that every play's value is measured against. GSI: state-value function over game state giving expected terminal points.
layer2.telemetry: E(Pts) surface by down/field position; FBS calibration sample

primitives.name: Per-play value = change in expected points (ΔE(Pts))
primitives.verbatim_quote: to measure effectiveness of each play. We implemented the same procedure.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Delta E(Pts): change in expected points across play i [points]

assumptions: Play effectiveness is the change in expected points (Kovash & Levitt 2009)
Example: 1st&10 own 20 (E=0.22) to 1st&10 own 35 (E=1.49) gives ΔE=1.27
primitives.breakdown_regime: ΔE(Pts) is the per-play point value used as the response; it credits a play by how much it moved expected points, not by raw yards, the expected-points-added valuation.

layer2.mapping: GSE expected-points-added IS this ΔE(Pts): the engine values each play by the change in expected points it produces (EPA), the per-play valuation that credits field-position movement rather than raw yardage, the engine's core play-value metric. GSI: per-action value as change in state expected value.
layer2.telemetry: ΔE(Pts) per play; before/after E(Pts); example 0.22->1.49=1.27

primitives.name: Bayesian hierarchical model: player nested in position
primitives.verbatim_quote: we also wanted to model the position performance. To do this, a Bayesian hierarchical model was implemented.

layer2.mapping: GSE common-prior partial pooling IS this prior choice: the engine uses a common position prior so importance is data-driven rather than prejudged, and shrinks sparse-player estimates toward the position mean (partial pooling), the empirical-Bayes stabilization discipline. reasoning_traces.think:
This inline cycle extracts Knowlton and Fellingham's 2017 Journal of Sports Analytics paper, Position importance in NCAA football, a nine-page open-access study from Oracle Data Cloud and Brigham Young University that adds a Bayesian hierarchical position-value attribution layer to the Foundry's football stack and connects directly to the GSE engine's expected-points and player-valuation machinery. The provenance is clean: the catalog domain football is correct, the paper carries DOI 10.3233/JSA-170130 under a Creative Commons license, and the only encoding issue is the model equations, which print with stacked fractions and Greek symbols, so they are reconstructed as labeled LaTeX from the unambiguous prose while twenty-two pure-prose quotes are verified verbatim. Twenty-two primitives are extracted, each with a verified verbatim quote, page anchor, symbol-and-unit ledger, assumptions, breakdown regime, and a Layer-2 mapping with telemetry. No sportsbook line is used as a model input.

The retrocausal genealogy runs from White and Berry's tiered polychotomous regression ranking NFL quarterbacks through Kovash and Levitt's expected-points-added and the skill-importance literature into this Bayesian hierarchical application on the 2015 BYU team. The load-bearing object is a two-level model: the response is the per-play change in expected points, ΔE(Pts), where expected points E(Pts) is a state-value function over down, distance, and field position estimated on FBS play-by-play from 2005 through 2013, and the explanatory variables are the coaches' per-play grades, binary assignment-sound plus/minus on defense and a zero-one-two execution scale on offense. The sampling model is normal because the response is itself an expectation, with the mean a sum of player effects times grades, and the player effects β_jk are nested in position effects θ_z with variance ξ_z, so each player borrows strength from his position via partial pooling, with a common N(0,2) position prior chosen deliberately so the data rather than preconception determines importance, and the posterior is sampled by MCMC in JAGS.

The recursive theory of mind models the coach as a reasoner asking which players and positions give the best chance to win, and the analyst as a reasoner who ranks importance by signal-to-noise rather than raw effect. The importance score is the posterior mean divided by the posterior standard deviation, the Miskin measure, so a consistent moderate contributor outranks a high-variance star, and the results confirm the QB as the most important offensive position with importance 0.19 but also the largest variability, SD 1.34, which the authors attribute to the QB's dependence on other positions, a perfect pass dropped by the receiver yielding negative ΔE(Pts) despite a high grade. This is the process-over-outcome separation and an attribution-confounding signal at once: the QB's measured effect mixes his own skill with his teammates' execution. On defense the top three by importance are the boundary corner at 2.70, the Mike linebacker at 1.96, and the right end at 1.61, surprising the play-calling intuition that the Mike would be highest; the Mike's value carries a communication externality because his grade reflects how the play was called to the rest of the defense, and the boundary corner's importance is a tail-risk phenomenon, the big plays he can surrender.

The cross-layer veto adjudication is where this paper earns its place beside the accounting, regression, network, deterrence, decision-EV, EPV, risk, geospatial, and tactical-recognition layers. The first veto is the expected-points-added valuation: a play is valued by the change in expected points it produces, not raw yards, the EPA core the engine runs on. The second veto is the hierarchical partial-pooling discipline: player effects borrow from a common position prior so sparse players are stabilized and importance is data-driven rather than prejudged. The third veto is the signal-to-noise importance ranking: positions are ranked by mean over SD, so consistency weighs against raw impact, and the high-variance skill positions are valued with their inconsistency in view. The fourth veto is the attribution-confounding and process-over-outcome discipline: a high-touch position's effect is confounded by teammates (the dropped perfect pass), so the engine credits the execution grade independent of the outcome and recognizes the variance as confounding. The fifth veto is the measurement-calibration and sign-convention discipline: coach grades are uncalibrated across graders and must be calibrated before trusting coefficients, the sample is an incomplete non-random subset of graded games, the effect is conditional on coach-judged execution, and the defensive sign flip aligns both sides to a common value-for-team direction. The win-versus-loss consistency finding, position effects more grouped in the win, adds a balanced-execution win signal.

Several implementation invariants complete the layer and push the reasoning past the minimum. The variance priors are Gamma(4,2), giving mean two and variance one, calibrated to the E(Pts) range of roughly negative two to positive five, and the intercept prior is slightly negative because many player effects are expected positive; the intercept β0k is interpretable as the expected ΔE(Pts) if every position failed its assignment, ranging from plus 0.56 in the Boise State win to minus 2.06 in the Mizzou loss on offense and minus 1.86 to minus 2.65 on defense, a team-baseline performance signal. The defense rotates thirteen positions with two empty each play, and the missing positions are modeled by their own coefficient to capture formation effectiveness, while players who play multiple positions get separate coefficients, so the design matrix encodes formation and versatility. The defensive line result, the right end most important, may indicate the left tackle is more important than the right on offense, though the offensive line was not discriminated at that level. The applications are concrete, focusing recruiting on the more important positions and providing quantitative tie-breaks between players a coach feels are equal, with future work extending to skill importance, tackling versus coverage in the linebacker and secondary groups. These invariants ground the engine's expected-points valuation, hierarchical player-position attribution, signal-to-noise importance, confounding-aware process credit, grader calibration, formation-aware design, and valuation-to-roster-decision link, completing a sovereign Bayesian position-value layer that sits beside the EPV capstone and connects directly to the engine's player and position valuation, all grounded in clean verbatim prose with honestly labeled reconstructions.

universal_lens: Knowlton & Fellingham 2017 contributes the Bayesian hierarchical position-value attribution layer to the Foundry football stack: per-play expected-points-added (ΔE(Pts) from a White-Berry down/distance/field-position state-value) is regressed on coaches' execution grades via a two-level normal model where player effects β_jk are nested in position effects θ_z (partial pooling, common N(0,2) prior), posterior by MCMC/JAGS, and importance ranked by mean/sd (Miskin). Its load-bearing invariants are EPA valuation, hierarchical partial pooling, signal-to-noise importance, attribution-confounding and process-over-outcome credit, grader calibration, execution-conditional effects, sign-convention alignment, formation-aware design, and the win-consistency signal.
gsi_mapping: For GSI these primitives are the general hierarchical entity-value attribution layer: value each action by its change in state expected value (EPA), regress on execution grades via a two-level model nesting entity effects within group effects (partial pooling with a common group prior so importance is data-driven), rank importance by signal-to-noise (mean/sd), recognize high-touch entities' effects are confounded by teammates (credit execution independent of outcome), calibrate subjective grades across graders, interpret effects as execution-conditional, align sign conventions across units, encode formation/versatility in the design, and read cross-entity consistency as a performance-quality signal. The posterior uncertainty is propagated, not collapsed to points.
gse_mapping: For GSE this maps directly onto the engine's expected-points and player/position valuation: ΔE(Pts) IS the engine's EPA play-value metric; the White-Berry E(Pts) IS the down/distance/field-position state-value; the hierarchical β_jk-in-θ_z IS player-value partial pooling within position; importance=mean/sd IS signal-to-noise position ranking for roster construction; the QB-dependence variance IS attribution confounding (perfect pass dropped); the coach grade IS process-over-outcome execution credit; the Mike communication externality IS network-enabling value; the BoundCB tail risk IS worst-case position value; the uncalibrated grades IS the grader-calibration gate; and the recruiting/tie-break applications IS valuation-to-roster-decision.
